summary: This version of the Restaurant class adds a placeOrder method that only accepts orders at 11:00 AM or later. Rather than asking the system directly what time it is, the class receives a Clock it can be told about, so tests can hand it any time they like.

lines.code: private static final LocalTime ORDER_OPEN_TIME = LocalTime.of(11, 0);
lines.text: Opening time is stored once as a named constant instead of being written as 11 inside the comparison, so the rule is stated in one obvious place.
The clock is the external dependency the class cannot control, so it is held as a field rather than being reached for at the moment it is needed. This is what makes the time swappable in a test.
The no-argument constructor is what real code uses; it quietly supplies the system clock so ordinary callers never have to think about clocks at all.
This second constructor is the door the test walks through: it hands in a fixed clock so the "before 11" and "after 11" scenarios can both be exercised on demand.
The spice level method from the earlier restaurant example still belongs here; the book leaves it as a placeholder to keep the focus on the new ordering feature.
Passing the clock to LocalTime.now() is the whole trick. Calling LocalTime.now() with no argument would read the real machine time and make this method untestable.
